newsitem.title: USA: PSE&G resigns from industry pollution group.
newsitem.headline: PSE&G resigns from industry pollution group.

text.p: Public Service Electric & Gas Co said Thursday it has moved to resign from the Utility Air Regulatory Group.

The Public Service Enterprise Group subsidiary said the resignation follows its intervention in the group's challenge of recently adopted NOx control requirements under Title IV of the federal Clean Air Act.
The utility intervened on the side of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency calling its proposals cost effective and reasonable, PSE&G spokesman Mark Brownstein explained.
The EPA proposals are at least a start, he continued, saying they are "below the minimum needed (to protect the U.S.) Northeast."

Previously, PSE&G president Lawrence R. Codey pointed out that one reason the utility has pushed NOx control is existing technology provides CO2 benefits "automatically" along with reduced particulate emissions.
He told Reuters the cost of such controls is "not going to change the dispatch" of electric power in a competitive market, adding it would be "a couple mills per kilowatthour."
Making the investment may mean a smaller decline in power prices with deregulation, he said, but it would be better than raising rates later to clean up NOx -- and other -- emissions.

Noting resignations from the Utility Air Regulatory Group that started with the debate over acid rain in the 1980s, Brownstein said PSE&G feels the industry association is no longer an effective voice and "there's no reason to pay dues."
He noted that the latest Utility Air Regulatory Group resignation was another northeast utility, Boston Edison Co.
He said the "forums we need to communicate with other utilities exist elsewhere," and cited the "Class of 85," a group formed during the acid rain debate that PSE&G has already joined.

The utility released the text of a letter Stanley LaBruna, its vice-president, environmental health and safety, sent to Dr. Charles H. Goodman, a Southern Co vice president who is chairman of the Utility Air Regulatory Group.
It said "PSE&G takes this step to avoid a prolonged and ultimately pointless discussion of what to do when a UARG member takes a position in opposition to UARG."
Noting the group had "truly represented the views of the utility industry on matters pertaining to federal air quality regulation," he wrote "Sadly, this is no longer true.
UARG's decline began with the Acid Rain debate, when the association's aggressive pro-coal position, taken at the expense of many members, caused a number of members to resign.
"The decline continues as UARG takes purported 'utility industry' positions on matters where sharp differences among UARG members exist.

"By choosing sides in regional debates over the transport of ozone and other pollutants, the proposed federal health standards for ozone and particulate matter, or the level of NOx control necessary to prevent Acid Rain, UARG has relegated itself to a partisan role representing a narrow set of interests," LaBruna wrote.
